title: How Companies Can Find New Value in Existing Materials
gist: BCG argues circularity is a resource-productivity and value-retention strategy, not waste management: EU electronics and appliances hold over €65B of critical minerals, end-of-use flows (~€9B/yr) exceed EU electronics manufacturing needs (~€6B/yr), and refurbishment/remanufacturing can cut manufacturing costs 60-70% and add 5+ points of margin. Value leaks through poor processing, misaligned incentives (tonnage-paid recyclers, unit-based sales) and missing condition data, so CEOs should appoint a single owner, follow the value hierarchy, and build data/AI and partner ecosystems now.

themes.theme: Hidden resource balance sheet in EU electronics

insights.claim: Appliances and consumer electronics in use across the EU hold critical minerals (copper, aluminum, rare earths, precious metals) worth more than €65 billion in stock.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: The installed base of consumer goods is a sizable domestic mineral reserve for a Europe that imports most raw critical minerals.
insights.quote: collectively worth more than €65 billion in stock across the EU
insights.locator: These products contain critical minerals—copper, aluminum

insights.claim: EU products reaching end of use each year contain about €9 billion of critical-mineral value, exceeding the roughly €6 billion of critical minerals EU electronics manufacturing requires annually.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: In principle Europe's end-of-use electronics stream could more than cover domestic electronics manufacturing's mineral needs, reducing import dependence.
insights.quote: contain about €9 billion of that critical-mineral value, more than the roughly €6 billion of critical minerals EU electronics manufacturing requires every year
insights.locator: These products contain critical minerals—copper, aluminum

insights.claim: Because Europe imports most finished electronics (under 1% of smartphones and under 20% of vacuum cleaners sold there are made locally) but the products stay in Europe until end of use, Europe accumulates more mineral value at end of life than its own production consumes.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Import-heavy regions become net 'mineral sinks' — an under-appreciated urban-mining advantage for import-dependent economies.
insights.quote: fewer than 1% of smartphones and fewer than 20% of vacuum cleaners sold there are made locally
insights.locator: Europe imports most of its finished electronics

insights.claim: End-of-use washing machines in the EU contain about €0.5 billion in critical minerals, roughly 70% of the €0.7 billion required by EU washing-machine production each year; about 75% of large appliances sold in Europe are made domestically.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: In domestically produced categories, recovered stock could supply most of the materials for new goods, cutting both cost and import reliance.
insights.quote: Washing machines, for example, contain about €0.5 billion in critical minerals, roughly 70% of the €0.7 billion required by EU production each year
insights.locator: Europe imports most of its finished electronics

insights.claim: BCG modeling shows demand for critical minerals running at 120% to 250% of forecast supply through 2040, making circularity a resilience lever amid price volatility and supply constraints.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Persistent structural supply deficits support critical-mineral prices and raise the strategic value of secondary supply and recovery capacity.
insights.quote: BCG modeling shows demand for critical minerals at 120% to 250% of forecast supply through 2040
insights.locator: In macroeconomic terms, gains could be substantial

themes.theme: Europe's e-waste leakage is a processing, not collection, problem

insights.claim: Only about 43% of European e-waste is formally collected versus a 65% EU target, and critical minerals account for 75% of the value in that stream.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Most of the value in e-waste is in critical minerals, so collection shortfalls translate directly into lost strategic material.
insights.quote: Only about 43% of European e-waste is formally collected, against a 65% EU target, and critical minerals account for 75% of the value in that stream
insights.locator: Today, only part of this value

insights.claim: The 57% of European e-waste missing from formal collection is not hoarded at home: just 13 of the average 74 electrical items in European households are unused, and large-appliance collection rates are high.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Policy aimed at 'drawer devices' misses the real leak; the fix is in channels and processing.
insights.quote: The missing 57% is not sitting in people’s homes
insights.locator: Today, only part of this value

insights.claim: European e-waste leaks into informal channels where it is downcycled: an estimated 13% goes to scrap-metal channels that recover bulk steel but lose refrigerants, plastics and critical minerals, around 8% goes into residual waste, and about 5% is reported as illegally exported.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Scrap-metal routing destroys critical-mineral value; formal recovery operators with better processing stand to gain share as regulation tightens.
insights.quote: an estimated 13% of European e-waste is absorbed by scrap metal channels that recover bulk steel but lose refrigerants, plastics, and critical minerals
insights.locator: Instead, the problem is often one

insights.claim: Recyclers are paid by tonnage processed, which rewards recovering bulk metal over critical minerals even though critical minerals hold 75% of the material value in e-waste.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Misaligned recycler incentives are a structural barrier; business models that pay for value recovered rather than tonnage could unlock trapped mineral value.
insights.quote: recyclers are paid by tonnage processed; this rewards recovery of bulk metal over that of the critical minerals
insights.locator: There are trade-offs, however

themes.theme: Value hierarchy: keep products whole before recycling

insights.claim: Circular value follows a hierarchy — preserving product life through design; then reuse, resale, repair, refurbishment and product-as-a-service; then component harvesting, remanufacturing and finally recycling — and higher tiers capture far more value.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Recycling is the lowest-value exit; companies and investors should prioritize life-extension and resale models over pure material recovery.
insights.quote: Circular value has a hierarchy: preserving product life through design
insights.locator: Circular value has a hierarchy

insights.claim: A secondhand smartphone sells for about €200 to €600, versus only about €5 for its recovered material.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: A ~40–120x value gap means refurbishment/resale platforms dwarf recycling economics for consumer devices.
insights.quote: the value of a secondhand smartphone in sales is about €200 to €600, compared with only about €5 for its recovered material
insights.locator: Circular value has a hierarchy

insights.claim: Companies should locate value 'cliffs' — points where a product's worth collapses by an order of magnitude — for each priority product and material cluster, and decide which products are economically worth recovering.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Mapping value cliffs turns circularity from a sustainability initiative into a targeted capital-allocation exercise.
insights.quote: points at which a product’s worth collapses by an order of magnitude
insights.locator: Establish the value of priority products

insights.claim: Circularity is mischaracterized as end-of-life waste management; it is actually a resource-productivity and value-retention strategy for monetizing value already embedded in products, components and materials.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Reframes circularity from a cost/compliance center to a margin and supply-security lever.
insights.quote: circularity is in fact a resource-productivity and value-retention strategy
insights.locator: Too often seen as an approach

themes.theme: Returns and ownership models decide value capture

insights.claim: About 60% to 70% of end-of-use washing machines can technically be reused or refurbished, yet only around 1% to 2% of collected machines are resold.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: A massive gap between technical and realized reuse signals a large untapped refurbishment market gated by reverse logistics and condition data.
insights.quote: about 60% to 70% of end-of-use washing machines can technically be reused or refurbished. Yet only around 1% to 2% of collected machines are resold
insights.locator: The second strategic imperative

insights.claim: Some commercial pay-per-use washing-machine models earn margins more than 15 percentage points higher per machine than one-off sales, and embedded material value as a share of lifetime revenue is about four times lower under a service model.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Product-as-a-service can structurally lift margins while diluting raw-material cost exposure.
insights.quote: some commercial pay-per-use models have margins more than 15 percentage points higher per machine than those of one-off sales
insights.locator: Washing machines again provide an illustration

insights.claim: Retaining ownership keeps products on the balance sheet, ties up capital, spreads revenue over time rather than booking it up front, and can cannibalize new-product sales.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating firms shifting to service models should expect near-term revenue deferral and higher capital intensity before margin gains show.
insights.quote: retaining ownership keeps products on the company’s balance sheet, tying up capital and spreading revenue over time
insights.locator: There are trade-offs, however

insights.claim: In manufacturing and retail, payments are frequently made by units shipped, so a product kept in use is one not sold — a commercial incentive that works against circularity.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Unit-volume incentive structures must be redesigned before circular models can scale inside incumbents.
insights.quote: payments are frequently made by units shipped, so a product kept in use is one not sold
insights.locator: There are trade-offs, however

insights.claim: Circularity priorities differ by sector: mechanical engineering should retain installed-base value via repair, refurbishment and remanufacturing; construction value sits in renovation/retrofit and higher-quality recycling of concrete, steel, aluminum, glass, wood and plastics.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Aftermarket service revenue on installed bases and retrofit activity are the near-term circular profit pools in industrials and building.
insights.locator: Circularity’s starting points also differ by sector

insights.claim: In mobility the incremental opportunity is component remanufacturing and battery and material recovery (repair is already an established aftermarket); in energy it is life extension, component reuse and second-life batteries; in textiles it is resale, rental, repair and ultimately fiber-to-fiber recycling.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Battery recovery and second-life batteries emerge as cross-sector opportunities spanning mobility and energy.
insights.quote: the incremental opportunity lies in component remanufacturing and battery and material recovery
insights.locator: In the mobility sector, auto repair

insights.claim: BCG and BDI research estimates Germany's circular-economy gross value added could reach €130 billion by 2045, twice today's €65 billion, with roughly €33 billion in investment.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Signals a sizable domestic investment theme in German industrial circularity over two decades.
insights.locator: In macroeconomic terms, gains could be substantial

insights.claim: In Germany, an estimated €7 billion in one-off investments made possible by current regulatory and market trends could generate up to €100 billion by 2045, meaning deep structural disruption is not needed to capture circular value.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Most of the prize is reachable with modest capex under existing rules — high-ROI near-term opportunities rather than system redesign.
insights.quote: an estimated €7 billion in one-off investments generating up to €100 billion by 2045
insights.locator: Enhanced coordination, infrastructure, and market development

insights.claim: Five German segments — mobility, mechanical engineering, construction, energy and textiles, together 62% of national industrial value added — could use circularity to cut import dependency on rare earths by 20% and strategic battery materials by 10% by 2045 versus baseline, even with higher demand.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Circularity is a partial geopolitical hedge against rare-earth and battery-material import dependence, though it does not eliminate it.
insights.quote: import dependency on rare earths and strategic battery materials could be reduced by 20% and 10%, respectively
insights.locator: A similar pattern can be seen in German industry

themes.theme: Five-move CEO agenda and enabling infrastructure

insights.claim: Refurbishment and remanufacturing can deliver about 15% savings on materials and 60% to 70% lower manufacturing costs, adding more than five percentage points to margins.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Circular lines can be materially margin-accretive, mostly via cost savings in the near term.
insights.quote: about 15% savings on materials and 60% to 70% lower manufacturing costs through refurbishment and remanufacturing—adding more than five percentage points to margins
insights.locator: In macroeconomic terms, gains could be substantial

insights.claim: Circularity frequently fails on organization rather than technology because design, returns, recycling and procurement savings sit in separate functions; one executive should own design, service, returns and sourcing with a numerical target.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Firms with a single accountable circularity owner are more likely to realize the economics; a useful governance tell for investors.
insights.quote: Circularity frequently fails on organization, not technology
insights.locator: Put one executive in charge

insights.claim: Returned assets cannot be traded unless condition can be assessed and priced, so shared data standards (condition grades for electronics, machinery part specs, building-material quality classes) matter at least as much as physical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Data/grading standards and platforms are a key enabler and potential chokepoint in secondary markets.
insights.quote: Data standards, in other words, matter at least as much as physical infrastructure
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the ability to scale

insights.claim: The EU is phasing in a Digital Product Passport (DPP) recording origin, material composition, components and repair/recycling information; together with condition data and AI-assisted sorting and grading, it enables returns to be priced and routed automatically.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Traceability, DPP compliance and AI grading tools are a growing software/services market tied to circularity.
insights.locator: Product data requirements support circularity

insights.claim: Recommended circularity KPIs are retained value per unit of resource, return-flow capture, revenue beyond first sale, margin on circular lines, customer lifetime value and primary-material exposure avoided, with economics judged on product-lifetime margins rather than first-sale revenue.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Gives analysts concrete metrics to assess whether a company's circularity claims create economic value.
insights.locator: Make data and AI the operating backbone

insights.claim: Advanced economies' funds allocated to critical minerals reached about $65 billion in 2025, yet less than 20% have been used, making public-sector vehicles an under-used source of circularity financing.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Large undeployed public capital could subsidize early circular investments; firms that tap it gain a cost-of-capital edge.
insights.quote: the funds that advanced economies have allocated to critical minerals reached about $65 billion in 2025, yet less than 20% have been used
insights.locator: Line up partners and investors

insights.claim: The European Environment Agency estimates 17 circular-economy measures could cut the EU's consumption-based emissions by around 22%.
insights.speaker: Patrick Herhold
insights.so_what: Environmental co-benefits strengthen the regulatory tailwind behind circular models.
insights.quote: 17 circular economy measures could cut the EU’s consumption-based emissions by around 22%
insights.locator: While accessing these benefits remains
